completion_reason: Three material architecture-integration decisions remain around reconnectable events, reproducible model selection, and secure workflow credential binding.

questions.label: Reconnectable event delivery
questions.context: The durable host continues accepted work after browsers or Electron disconnect. An event cursor is a saved position—such as event 418—that lets a reconnecting client request everything it missed after that point.
questions.evidence: `packages/central-client/index.mjs` is the shared command boundary for Electron, HTTP, and WebSocket clients; `services/nexus-node/src/nexus-node.mjs` remains authoritative after clients close; and `adapters/runtime-adapters/src/sqlite-store.mjs` already persists events in SQLite WAL. The missing decision is what every client may rely on after reconnecting.
questions.impact: This determines whether Work, Workflows, and Runs can recover coherent progress and approval state after network loss. Long term, it sets one integration contract for desktop, browser, and local API clients instead of transport-specific recovery behavior.
questions.question: What event-recovery guarantee should NexusCentral provide when a client reconnects?

choices.consequence: Clients resume from their last acknowledged event cursor, while an authoritative snapshot closes any retention gap; this adds cursor and retention rules now but gives every client deterministic recovery long term.
Reconnects fetch current state and receive only new events; implementation is simpler now, but transient logs and intermediate transitions may be unavailable to clients and integrations.
Clients receive events only while connected and must manually refresh after loss; this is cheapest immediately but produces fragile UX and unsuitable automation semantics.

questions.recommendation_reason: The host and event store are already durable, so cursor replay exposes that durability consistently and prevents disconnects from hiding approval or terminal transitions.

questions.label: Workflow model identity
questions.context: A model reference is the identifier stored in a published workflow to select inference later. It may point to a stable model revision, a changeable alias such as “best-coding,” or only a capability requirement.
questions.evidence: `packages/contracts/index.mjs` spans several provider protocol families, while `kits/providers-kit/index.mjs` owns provider profiles and `kits/routing-kit/index.mjs` owns capability matching and fallback. Without a shared reference rule, the same workflow can silently execute against materially different models.
questions.impact: This changes workflow records, Router resolution, run provenance, and replay validation now. Long term, it decides whether workflows are reproducible while still permitting operators to upgrade models intentionally.
questions.question: What model reference should a published workflow store for each inference stage?

choices.consequence: Store an immutable provider/model revision or verified local artifact identity together with allowed fallback constraints; records are richer now, but runs remain reproducible and fallback stays explicit.
Store a versioned alias whose mapping is published separately; upgrades are convenient and auditable, but replay also depends on retaining every alias version.
Store context, modality, tool, and performance needs and let Router choose at runtime; portability is highest, but identical workflow versions may yield materially different behavior.
Store the provider’s current model string; integration is simplest, but provider-side changes can silently alter results and undermine replay evidence.

questions.recommendation_reason: Pinned identity preserves immutable run evidence, while explicit routing constraints retain the locked queue failover behavior without silently changing the workflow’s intended model.

questions.label: Workflow credential binding
questions.context: A credential binding is a secret-free name in a workflow—such as “production-bedrock”—that the host resolves to an authorized credential when a run starts. The workflow never contains the secret itself.
questions.evidence: `kits/providers-kit/index.mjs` keeps profiles secret-free and leaves credentials in host secure storage; `packages/composition/index.mjs` separates domain decisions from adapter I/O; and `adapters/runtime-adapters/src/harness-executors.mjs` executes stages that may require external providers or tools. Multi-user workflows therefore need an explicit ownership and resolution boundary.
questions.impact: This determines how workflow definitions remain portable, how collaborators are prevented from using credentials they do not own, and what credential identity is recorded in immutable run provenance. It also shapes future rotation and migration behavior.
questions.question: How should a published workflow bind stages to credentials or secret-backed environments?

choices.consequence: Workflows store secret-free binding names; the host resolves a binding at run start only if the workflow and initiating actor are authorized, recording a non-secret credential version in provenance. This adds policy checks now but supports rotation, collaboration, and portability safely.
Every run uses bindings owned by the workflow owner regardless of who starts it; scheduled execution is straightforward, but collaborators can indirectly consume the owner’s access and budget.
Each run resolves bindings from the user who starts it; accountability is direct, but schedules and shared workflows fail when that user is absent or lacks matching credentials.
All workflows share deployment-wide provider secrets; setup is simplest, but isolation, attribution, rotation, and least-privilege controls remain weak.

questions.recommendation_reason: Logical bindings preserve the existing secret-free domain boundary while supporting scheduled work, per-user authorization, credential rotation, and auditable multi-user collaboration.
